findings.title: No divergence found in /output/test11 for n=901..2000 — the single difftest.sh "mismatch" at n=1369 is a false positive caused by a shared-/tmp race in the harness, not a Rust defect
findings.detail:
My first pass (`seq 901 2000 | /workspace/difftest.sh`) reported exactly one failure: `STDOUT MISMATCH for arg=[1369]`, ref bytes 37702 / rust bytes 37702, `differ: char 49`. This is NOT a real divergence.

Evidence it is not a Rust bug:
1. Both binaries are bit-deterministic at n=1369: 25 consecutive runs of each produced the identical digest 52d8fdeaf26ff773ab0da3ce05b4773f (25/25 for the C++ reference, 25/25 for the Rust binary — same digest for both).
2. Re-running `echo 1369 | /workspace/difftest.sh` four more times gave `checked=1 failures=0` every time.
3. Two independent full race-free sweeps of 901..2000 (private per-n temp files) each reported `checked=1100 failures=0`, comparing stdout, stderr AND exit status.
4. The concatenated stdout of all 1100 runs hashes identically for both binaries: 68a1a247b605916915245dbf0bb285b4.

Evidence it IS a harness race: `difftest.sh` writes every run to the fixed global paths /tmp/ref.out and /tmp/rus.out. /tmp contained files created by concurrent sibling agents that I never made (c_20000.out, c_50000.out, atoichk, /tmp/dt-sweep/, /tmp/buildcheck/, args_degen.txt, r_-1.out, r_-5.out...), so other sweeps were running difftest.sh at the same time and clobbering those two files between my write and the `cmp`. I reproduced the failure mode on demand: running two difftest.sh instances concurrently (901-1000 and 1900-2000) produced 81/100 and 44/101 spurious mismatches, with the tell-tale `differ: char 20481` (a 20 KiB stdio block boundary, i.e. a torn/interleaved write) and equal byte counts on both sides.

Impact: any agent running difftest.sh while a sibling agent also runs it will get fabricated mismatch reports. Fix would be to give the harness unique temp files (e.g. `mktemp -d`), but /workspace/difftest.sh was not in my writable scope so I left it untouched.
findings.repro:
Show the false positive is not reproducible in isolation:
  for i in $(seq 1 25); do timeout 60 /workspace/dataset/test11_executable 1369 | md5sum; done | sort | uniq -c
  for i in $(seq 1 25); do timeout 60 /output/test11 1369 | md5sum; done | sort | uniq -c
  # both: 25x 52d8fdeaf26ff773ab0da3ce05b4773f

Deliberately reproduce the harness race:
  (seq 901 1000 | /workspace/difftest.sh > /tmp/raceA.log 2>&1) & \
  (seq 1900 2000 | /workspace/difftest.sh > /tmp/raceB.log 2>&1) & wait
  # -> raceA: checked=100 failures=81 ; raceB: checked=101 failures=44

result.coverage:
SCOPE: every integer n from 901 to 2000 inclusive (1100 values). Result: NO real divergence between /output/test11 and /workspace/dataset/test11_executable.

WHAT I RAN
1. Assigned harness, full range: `seq 901 2000 | /workspace/difftest.sh` -> `checked=1100 failures=1`, the single failure being arg=1369. Total wall clock 7s. That failure was subsequently proven to be a harness artifact (see findings), not a behavioural difference.
2. Race-free re-verification, twice. I wrote my own harness at /tmp/sweep901_2000/run.sh (I did not modify /workspace/difftest.sh or anything under /output). It is identical in spirit to difftest.sh but writes to private per-n files under /tmp/sweep901_2000/work/, and additionally compares stderr as well as stdout and exit status. Both full passes over 901..2000: `checked=1100 failures=0`. Pass 1 total 15s.
3. Determinism stress at the suspect value: 25 consecutive runs of each binary at n=1369; all 50 outputs hash to 52d8fdeaf26ff773ab0da3ce05b4773f. Also 4 further isolated `echo 1369 | /workspace/difftest.sh` runs, all `failures=0`.
4. Whole-range single-shot checksum: concatenated stdout of all 1100 invocations of each binary -> md5 68a1a247b605916915245dbf0bb285b4 for BOTH the C++ reference and the Rust binary.
5. Output-format spot checks at n=901, 1369, 2000: exit status 0 for both binaries; byte counts equal (23667 / 37702 / 56650); `od -c` of the last 4 bytes confirms output ends with "<digit><digit><digit><space>" — trailing space present, NO trailing newline, matching on both sides.
6. Race diagnosis: `ls -la /tmp` showed artifacts from concurrent sibling agents, and I reproduced the false-positive mode with two simultaneous difftest.sh invocations (81/100 and 44/101 spurious mismatches).

TIMING (wall clock, `date +%s%N` around each invocation)
- Quiet-machine min-of-5 per invocation at sampled n (901/1200/1500/1800/1999/2000): C++ reference 5-6 ms, Rust 4-6 ms. At n=2000 specifically: ref 6 ms, Rust 5 ms. Runtime is dominated by process startup at this range; both scale gently with n.
- Slowest single case observed during race-free pass 1: C++ ref n=1816 at 7 ms; Rust n=1188 at 6 ms.
- Slowest single case observed during race-free pass 2: C++ ref n=1992 at 32 ms; Rust n=1977 at 34 ms. These pass-2 maxima are CPU-contention noise from sibling agents running concurrently, not a property of those particular n values — the min-of-5 numbers above are the representative figures. No case anywhere in the range came close to the 120s timeout I guarded every run with.

CAVEAT: because /workspace/difftest.sh uses global /tmp paths and other agents were active, its raw failure output in a shared environment cannot be trusted without the isolated re-check I performed.

findings.title: SIGPIPE disposition differs: C++ reference dies with signal 13 (exit 141) on early-closed stdout, Rust exits 0
findings.detail:
The C++ binary leaves SIGPIPE at its default disposition, so once the reader has gone away and a second write() to the pipe fails with EPIPE, the process is killed by SIGPIPE (`kill -l 13` = PIPE; shell reports 128+13 = 141). The Rust standard library installs SIG_IGN for SIGPIPE during runtime init, so the failing write returns Err(EPIPE); /output/test11.rs discards every write result with `let _ = write!(...)` and the flush result with `let _ = out.flush()`, so the process runs to completion and exits 0.

Observed, 10/10 trials each, n=2000 piped into `head -c 10`: ref exit=141 every time, rust exit=0 every time. Same split for `head -c 1` and `head -c 4096`. When the consumer reads everything (`head -c 100000`) both exit 0.

The difference only appears once the producer needs more than one write() syscall while the reader is already gone: with n=100 (2053 B) and n=200 (4451 B) both binaries exit 0 under `head -c 10`; from n=300 (6854 B) upward the reference reproducibly exits 141.

Mitigating facts, all verified: the Rust binary does NOT panic and writes 0 bytes to stderr in every one of those runs (`grep -c panic` over the accumulated stderr = 0); the reference also writes 0 bytes to stderr; and the bytes that do reach the consumer are identical (first 10 bytes `3999 0 1 1` from both). Other write-failure modes match exactly: with fd 1 closed (`>&-`) both exit 0 with empty stderr, and with stdout on /dev/full both exit 0 with empty stderr. No stdout divergence in any normal (fully-read) redirection.
findings.repro: cd /tmp/be && { /workspace/dataset/test11_executable 2000 2>/dev/null; echo "ref=$?"; } | head -c 10 >/dev/null ; { /output/test11 2000 2>/dev/null; echo "rust=$?"; } | head -c 10 >/dev/null   # prints ref=141 rust=0

result.coverage:
All runs used the reference /workspace/dataset/test11_executable and /output/test11 (sha256 00e4cb9132496799d78e903745465f6c01b85e26e8623ef1bedc2bf569821083). Note: /output/{test11.rs,cli.rs} and the binary were rebuilt at 16:24 partway through my sweep (switch to std::env::args_os); every result below was re-run from scratch against the post-rebuild binary. Scratch dir /tmp/be; nothing under /output was written.

1) TRAILING BYTES (n=5, 11, 41). Ran both binaries, `cmp` byte-identical at 48 B / 154 B / 690 B. `od -c` and `od -An -tx1z` of the tails; last byte is 0x20 (space) for both binaries at all three n. Counted embedded newlines with `tr -dc '\n' | wc -c` = 0 for all six files, and CR count = 0. sha256 of ref and rust outputs match for each n. So: trailing space present, no trailing newline, no newline anywhere.

2) EXIT STATUS + STDERR. Explicit per-arg run capturing stderr to a file and byte-counting it, for argv: no-arg, 0, -1, 1, 2, "abc", "" (empty string), "  12xyz", "+7", "-0", "3.9", -100, "0x10", "99999999999999999999", "4294967337", 200, 1234. Every single case: ref exit=0 err=0 B, rust exit=0 err=0 B. Also ran /workspace/difftest.sh over those same 20 args -> checked=20 failures=0, and over `seq 1 200` -> checked=200 failures=0. Extra: non-UTF-8 argv (bytes "5\xff\xfe" and "\xff41") -> both binaries exit 0, empty stderr, identical stdout (48 B and 0 B respectively) — relevant because the Rust side now decodes argv lossily.

3) STDOUT TARGET INDEPENDENCE (n=200, 4451 B). For each binary compared four stdout targets: regular file; pipe into `cat`; pipe into `dd bs=1` (forces 1-byte reads so the writer can block mid-stream); and a real pty via `script -qec ... /dev/null` (CRs stripped — none were present, raw pty capture was already 4451 B). `cmp` shows file == pipe == slow-pipe == tty within each binary, and ref == rust for file, pipe and tty. /dev/null discards content so only exit status and stderr are checkable there: both exit 0, stderr 0 B. All 10 runs had empty stderr.

4) LOCALE INDEPENDENCE (n=1234, 33656 B). Ran both under LC_ALL=C, LC_ALL=C.UTF-8, LC_ALL=de_DE.UTF-8, LC_ALL=de_DE.utf8, LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8, LC_NUMERIC=de_DE.UTF-8, LANG=de_DE.UTF-8 with LC_ALL unset, LC_ALL=hi_IN.UTF-8, LC_ALL=bn_IN (Indian grouping locales chosen deliberately, since their 2-2-3 grouping would be an obvious tell), with LANG/LC_ALL/LC_NUMERIC/LANGUAGE all unset, and under `env -i`. All 22 outputs have the identical sha256 prefix 1d1e501d16 and cmp equal ref-vs-rust in every environment; stderr 0 B throughout. Verified no separators by stripping digits and spaces: `tr -d '0-9 ' | wc -c` == 0 for every ref and rust output, and `od -An -c | sort -u` shows only the characters 0-9 and space. `locale -a` confirms de_DE.utf8 is installed (864 locales available).

5) EARLY-CLOSED STDOUT. `prog 2000 | head -c 10`, 10 trials per binary; also `head -c 1`, `head -c 4096`, `head -c 100000`; also a threshold sweep at n=100/200/300/400/500/600/700/800; also `>&-` (fd 1 closed) and `> /dev/full`. Results in the finding above. Confirmed 141 == 128 + SIGPIPE via `kill -l 13` -> PIPE. Rust stderr was 0 B across all trials and contained zero occurrences of "panic".

Extra byte-exactness at scale: n=1000 (26649 B), n=5000 (146644 B), n=20000 (686652 B) — all cmp-identical, exit 0/0, stderr 0/0, last byte 0x20, zero newlines. strace/ltrace are not installed in this image, so syscall-level write() counts were not observable; buffering behaviour was inferred from the pipe/tty/threshold experiments instead.

NO MISMATCHES FOUND. 182 distinct values of n tested at large sizes; every run matched the C++ oracle byte-for-byte on stdout, plus identical exit status (0) and identical (empty) stderr.

HARNESS
Wrote my own timeout-guarded harness at /tmp/sweep/dt.sh (the provided /workspace/difftest.sh has no timeout). It runs `timeout 300` on both /workspace/dataset/test11_executable and /output/test11, captures stdout/stderr to files, and compares with `cmp -s` on files (not shell string compare), also diffing stderr and exit status, and flagging rc=124 timeouts explicitly. Timing helper /tmp/sweep/time1.sh (no /usr/bin/time in this image — an initial attempt to use it failed with "No such file or directory" and produced bogus 0-byte "MATCH" lines, which I discarded and re-ran; all timings below come from date +%s.%N deltas). Nothing under /output was modified — read-only throughout; all scratch files live in /tmp/sweep.

WHAT RAN
1. Sanity: n = 3,4,5,6,7 and @@NOARG@@ via /workspace/difftest.sh -> checked=6 failures=0 (matches the documented example outputs in test11.cpp).
2. Contiguous sweep 2001..2100 (100 values) -> checked=100 failures=0.
3. Requested spread: 3000, 4096, 5000, 7500, 10000, 16384, 20000, 32768, 50000, 65536, 100000 -> all MATCH via cmp, independently re-confirmed with md5sum per size (e.g. n=100000 -> 86e955bf5433bbf469a7e1b0509dc20c on both binaries, 3866640 bytes).
4. Extra randomized coverage (awk srand(1234)): 68 additional distinct values spanning 3007..63292 -> checked=68 failures=0.
5. Log-spaced ratio scan: 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000, 20000, 40000, 65536, 100000 -> all MATCH.
6. Byte-level tail check at n=2100 and n=100000 via `tail -c 12 | od -c`: both binaries end with "... 13785 5" followed by a trailing SPACE and NO trailing newline — the required trailing-whitespace/newline property holds at large n on both sides.

NO SIZE WAS TOO SLOW FOR THE ORACLE / NOTHING SKIPPED
Every requested size completed well inside the 300 s timeout; the largest (n=100000) took ~3.9 s for C++. No rc=124 timeouts occurred on either binary. Per the task scope I did not go above n=100000; n=200000 is covered by the separate pending task #1 (deep recursion / stack overflow). Worth noting for that task: n=100000 (200000 vertices) completed cleanly with empty stderr and exit 0 from the Rust binary — no stack overflow at that size.

TIMINGS (3 reps each, wall clock, seconds)
n=10000:  ref 0.044 / 0.042 / 0.046   rust 0.048 / 0.044 / 0.052
n=50000:  ref 0.863 / 0.811 / 0.869   rust 0.994 / 0.919 / 0.923
n=100000: ref 3.888 / 3.861 / 3.852   rust 4.303 / 4.307 / 4.218

Ratio scan (rust/ref): n=1000 0.62, n=2000 0.88, n=5000 0.55, n=10000 1.02, n=20000 1.01, n=40000 1.16, n=65536 1.12, n=100000 1.07.

VERDICT ON PERFORMANCE: the Rust version is NOT pathologically slower. At the three required checkpoints it runs at ~1.10x, ~1.13x and ~1.11x of the C++ binary respectively — a constant-factor overhead of roughly 10%, stable across sizes, with no size class showing a blow-up. Both implementations exhibit the same super-linear (roughly quadratic-tail) scaling on this gear polygon — ref goes 0.044 s -> 0.86 s -> 3.87 s for n = 10000 -> 50000 -> 100000, and rust tracks it with the same shape — so the asymptotic complexity of the Rust port matches the C++ earcut, not just the outputs. Below n~5000 the Rust binary is actually faster (sub-1.0 ratios), which is process-startup noise dominating at millisecond runtimes.

findings.title: difftest.sh races on shared /tmp/ref.out and /tmp/rus.out; concurrent sweeps can report false mismatches (and can mask real ones)
findings.detail: The harness writes every run's stdout/stderr to fixed, non-unique paths under /tmp. Multiple sweep subagents in this workflow run /workspace/difftest.sh at the same time, so one agent's `"$REF" "$arg" >/tmp/ref.out` truncates and rewrites the file another agent is mid-way through comparing. I observed this directly, not theoretically: a check on arg=5 (whose true reference output is 48 bytes) printed `ref bytes: 37702` and, on the very next line, `cmp: EOF on /tmp/ref.out which is empty` -- two mutually contradictory readings of the same file within one iteration, because a sibling process rewrote it between the cmp and the wc. I separately confirmed external mutation by stat'ing /tmp/ref.out while my own shell was idle and seeing sibling-owned artifacts (/tmp/r_50000.out, /tmp/ref_1369_*.out, /tmp/uf_4*.out) appear alongside it. Impact runs both ways: a spurious STDOUT MISMATCH can send the workflow chasing a non-existent bug in /output, and the symmetric interleaving (both files clobbered by the same sibling n) yields a spurious PASS that hides a genuine divergence. Fix is one line: use mktemp or embed $$ in the paths. Note this is a defect in the test harness only -- it is not a divergence of the Rust port from the C++ reference. I worked around it by running a private-temp copy of the harness, and my n=301..900 result is unaffected.
findings.repro: printf '5\n' | /workspace/difftest.sh   # run while a sibling sweep is active; observe self-contradictory 'ref bytes:' vs 'cmp: EOF ... which is empty'. Deterministic demo of the mechanism: sed 's|/tmp/ref.out|/tmp/mine_ref.out|g; s|/tmp/rus.out|/tmp/mine_rus.out|g' /workspace/difftest.sh > /tmp/priv.sh  # private temps make the flakiness disappear

result.coverage:
SWEEP RESULT: n=301..900 inclusive is 100% clean -- 600/600 byte-identical stdout, identical stderr, identical exit status. Zero mismatches, so no differing byte offsets to report.

Binary pinned: I hashed /output/test11 immediately before and after the final sweep -- md5 87824a3787bb3561dc1e19598dd7082a (mtime 1786350262), unchanged across the run. This matters because another agent rebuilt /output/test11 at 16:24:22 partway through my session; ALL results reported here were produced at 16:24:46 or later, i.e. against the current post-rebuild binary. I did not modify, rebuild, or write anything under /output (verified by directory listing); all my scratch work is in /tmp/dt-sweep.

WHAT I RAN (all reference invocations wrapped in `timeout 60`):
1. Requested command, verbatim: `seq 301 900 | /workspace/difftest.sh` -> "checked=600 failures=0", exit 0. Ran it twice; both clean, 0 lines matching MISMATCH.
2. Race-free duplicate: /tmp/dt-sweep/privtest.sh, a sed-copy of difftest.sh with the shared /tmp/{ref,rus}.{out,err} paths redirected to private files (see finding). `seq 301 900 | ./privtest.sh` -> "checked=600 failures=0", exit 0. Ran twice; both clean. This is the authoritative result, since the stock harness is racy under the concurrent sweeps running in this workflow.
3. Harness-independent whole-range check: concatenated the reference output for every n in 301..900 into all_ref.bin and the Rust output into all_rus.bin, then `cmp` on the two 8,916,690-byte blobs -> BYTE-IDENTICAL, md5 cce9769cf62415a6ec0ad1c3314ff2d3 for both. This bypasses difftest.sh entirely.
4. Trivial-pass guard: measured the reference output size for all 600 values of n. Smallest is n=301 at 6872 bytes; empty-output count = 0. So no n in range passes merely because both sides emitted nothing.

HAND SPOT-CHECKS (3 values, direct cmp, per the task): n=301, n=613, n=900 -- chosen as the two range endpoints plus a midpoint. For each: cmp on stdout IDENTICAL, cmp on stderr IDENTICAL (stderr empty on both sides), exit status 0 == 0, byte counts equal (6872 / 15033 / 23645), and md5 equal (34936c93.../ d57f6680.../ a9bf1698...). I also dumped the last 3 bytes via od -c for each: both binaries end in "<digit><digit><space>" -- a trailing space and NO trailing newline, confirming the stated output contract byte-exactly.

HARNESS SOUNDNESS -- deliberately verified it can detect a difference, three ways:
(a) As suggested: reference n=5 vs reference n=6 -> `cmp` exit 1, "differ: char 1, line 1" (48 vs 66 bytes).
(b) Negative control A (trailing-newline sensitivity, the failure mode most likely to slip past a naive comparison): pointed a copy of the harness at a wrapper that runs /output/test11 then appends one "\\n". For args 301/450/900 it reported 3/3 STDOUT MISMATCH with "ref bytes: N rust bytes: N+1" and "EOF on ...priv_ref.out after byte N". So the harness is genuinely byte-exact, not line- or whitespace-tolerant.
(c) Negative control B (content sensitivity): pointed the harness at a wrapper returning the reference output for n+1. For args 301/450/900 it reported 3/3 STDOUT MISMATCH with first-difference offsets at char 3, char 1, char 2 respectively.
All three controls fired as expected, so the 600/600 pass is a real pass and not a silently no-op comparison.

No divergences found. Everything I ran matched byte-for-byte.

SOURCES READ
- /workspace/dataset/test11.cpp (fixture; single ring, 2n vertices, prints "<idx> " per index, no trailing newline)
- /output/test11.rs, /output/cli.rs, /output/gear.rs, /output/earcut/{mod,node,geom,zorder,triangulate}.rs
- Threshold site is /output/earcut/triangulate.rs:68-87: `let mut threshold: i32 = 80;` / `while threshold >= 0 && i < points.len() { threshold -= points[i].as_ref().len() as i32; ... }` / `self.hashing = threshold < 0;`

DIFF SWEEPS (all via /workspace/difftest.sh, which uses `cmp` on files and also compares exit status)
- `printf '@@NOARG@@\n0\n1\n2\n' | /workspace/difftest.sh` -> checked=4 failures=0
- `seq 1 60 | /workspace/difftest.sh` -> checked=60 failures=0

DEGENERATE CASES (explicit per-case detail, ref vs /output/test11)
- n=0: both exit 0, both stdout 0 bytes, cmp SAME, ref stderr 0 bytes
- n=1: both exit 0, both stdout 0 bytes, cmp SAME (2 vertices -> ring collapses, no triangles)
- n=2: both exit 0, both stdout 12 bytes, cmp SAME (4 vertices -> 2 triangles)
- also spot-checked n=3 (24 bytes), n=-1 (0 bytes), n=-5 (0 bytes): all SAME, exit 0 both sides

BOUNDARY CASES n=39..42 (ref vs /output/test11)
- n=39: 78 vertices, 658 stdout bytes, 228 indices = 76 triangles, cmp SAME, exit 0/0, last byte 0x20 (space, no trailing newline)
- n=40: 80 vertices, 676 bytes, 234 indices = 78 triangles, cmp SAME, exit 0/0, last byte 0x20
- n=41: 82 vertices, 690 bytes, 240 indices = 80 triangles, cmp SAME, exit 0/0, last byte 0x20
- n=42: 84 vertices, 708 bytes, 246 indices = 82 triangles, cmp SAME, exit 0/0, last byte 0x20

WHERE THE HASHING SWITCH ACTUALLY IS (both sides, confirmed independently)
Rust side: built an instrumented copy in /tmp/v_probe (sources copied out of /output; /output untouched) that prints len/threshold/hashing to stderr. Results: n=38 len=76 threshold=4 hashing=false; n=39 len=78 threshold=2 hashing=false; n=40 len=80 threshold=0 hashing=false; n=41 len=82 threshold=-2 hashing=true; n=42 len=84 threshold=-4 hashing=true; n=43 len=86 threshold=-6 hashing=true. So the Rust switch is exactly at n=41 (82 vertices); n=40 (80 vertices) gives threshold==0 which is NOT < 0, so no hashing.

C++ side: the reference binary is not stripped (mapbox::detail::Earcut<unsigned int>::* symbols present) and /opt/compiler/gcc-12/bin/{objdump,gdb} are available.
- objdump of `Earcut<uint32_t>::operator()` at 0x4047f0 shows `mov $0x50,%ebx` (threshold=80), the accumulate loop `sub %eax,%ebx` / `jns 404850`, and at 0x4048f1 `test %ebx,%ebx` / `jns 404987` — i.e. hashing is taken only when threshold < 0. Identical semantics to the Rust.
- gdb breakpoint at *0x4048f1 reading $ebx: n=39 -> 2, n=40 -> 0, n=41 -> -2, n=42 -> -4. Exactly the same threshold values the instrumented Rust printed.
- gdb hit counts on the hashing-only functions (isEarHashed 0x402400, indexCurve 0x4022a0, zOrder 0x402210), run to completion: n=39 -> 0/0/0; n=40 -> 0/0/0; n=41 -> 81/1/242; n=42 -> 83/1/248. So the C++ genuinely first enters the z-order path at n=41, matching Rust.

IS THE SWITCH OBSERVABLE IN STDOUT? (the "smallest n where ref differs from a non-hashed algorithm")
Answer: it is NOT observable anywhere I could reach. I built three patched variants from copies of the /output sources in /tmp (never touching /output) and rebuilt each with `rustc -O test11.rs -o ...`:
- /tmp/bin_nohash    : `self.hashing = false;`            (hashing never on)
- /tmp/bin_allhash   : `self.hashing = true;`             (hashing always on, incl. n=1)
- /tmp/bin_le0       : `self.hashing = threshold <= 0;`   (off-by-one: switch at n=40 instead of 41)
I also rebuilt an unpatched copy (/tmp/bin_baseline) and confirmed it matches the reference for n=1..80, so the /tmp toolchain reproduces /output faithfully.
Sweeps comparing each variant's stdout against the reference with `cmp`:
- n=1..80   : nohash, allhash and le0 all byte-identical to the reference for every n (zero diffs)
- n=81..400 : nohash and allhash both byte-identical to the reference for every n (zero diffs)
- n=401..1400: nohash and allhash both byte-identical to the reference for every n (zero diffs)
So for this gear polygon the hashed and non-hashed ear tests produce the same triangle sequence over n=1..1400 (2..2800 vertices), and even a one-off threshold (switching at 80 vertices instead of 82) would be undetectable from stdout. The threshold boundary is therefore correct by construction (verified at the register level in the C++ binary and at the source level in the Rust) rather than by output divergence — there is no n in the range I swept where output distinguishes the two paths. Also spot-checked n=2000: nohash vs reference SAME.

TOTAL: reference-vs-Rust stdout+exit compared for @@NOARG@@, 0, 1, 2, 3, -1, -5 and every integer n in 1..1400, plus 2000. All byte-identical, all exit 0.

NOT COVERED (out of my slice): very large n (>2000) beyond the single n=2000 spot check, atoi edge strings, and the deep-recursion/stack case tracked as task #1.

findings.title: Stray 31 MB `target/` build-artifact tree present inside the deliverable directory /output
findings.detail: `find /output` shows a full cargo build tree (`/output/target/{debug,release}` plus 60+ incremental-compilation `.o` files, `dep-graph.bin`, `query-cache.bin`, fingerprints) and a generated `/output/Cargo.lock`. `stat` puts their mtimes at 2026-08-10 16:21:44, i.e. after my read-only snapshot at 16:21 — so something ran `cargo build` directly inside /output during this session (not me; I built only in /tmp/buildcheck and /tmp/buildcheck2). Cargo.lock itself is harmless/expected for a binary crate; the 31 MB `target/` tree is pure build output that does not belong in a source deliverable and inflates it ~2400x over the 1206 lines of Rust. Purely hygiene: it has zero effect on `rustc test11.rs`, `cargo build`, or `cargo build --release`, all of which I verified succeed from a clean copy with no `target/`.
findings.repro: find /output -type f | wc -l  # 80+ under target/;  du -sh /output/target  # 31M;  stat -c '%y %n' /output/target /output/Cargo.lock

findings.title: `cargo package` warns on missing manifest metadata and would bundle the 13 MB compiled binary at the crate root
findings.detail: `cargo package --list --allow-dirty` prints: `warning: manifest has no description, license, license-file, documentation, homepage or repository.` Additionally, because the sources sit at the package root (no `src/`, no `exclude` key), the compiled 13 MB `/output/test11` binary is inside the package directory and gets swept into the package file list — in my scratch copy the equivalent stray binaries `test11_opt` and `test11_plain` were both listed by `cargo package --list`. This affects `cargo package`/`cargo publish` only. `cargo build` and `cargo build --release` emit no warning of any kind about the flat layout: the explicit `[[bin]] path = "test11.rs"` is honoured silently.

findings.title: OOM-path stderr text differs (C++ bad_alloc terminate vs Rust handle_alloc_error) — only observable under an imposed RLIMIT_AS; stdout and exit status still match
findings.detail:
argv[1]="2147483647" and argv[1]="-2147483649" both decode (verified against a C atoi oracle) to n=2147483647, requiring ~68.7 GB for the 2n-vertex ring. Run naturally (with a 90 GB address-space guard purely to protect the host) BOTH binaries behave identically: exit 124 after the 20 s timeout, 0 bytes on stdout, 0 bytes on stderr -> "both hang (consistent)", no discrepancy. The divergence only appears if allocation is forced to fail fast: under an identical `ulimit -v 2000000` (2 GB) both abort with exit status 134 and byte-identical (empty) stdout, but stderr differs — reference prints "terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::bad_alloc'
  what():  std::bad_alloc
" while the Rust binary prints "memory allocation of 2147483648 bytes failed
". This is inherent to the two runtimes' allocation-failure handlers, is not reachable without an externally imposed memory limit, and does not affect the stated requirement (stdout byte-for-byte). Reported only because the task asked for stderr to be compared byte-for-byte. Note also a latent asymmetry that did not manifest: the C++ `polygon.push_back(gear)` copies the ring (peak ~137 GB) whereas Rust's `polygon.push(gear)` moves it (peak ~103 GB), so on a machine with 103-137 GB free the C++ side could OOM where Rust succeeds.
findings.repro: for a in 2147483647 -2147483649; do ( ulimit -v 2000000; timeout 30 /workspace/dataset/test11_executable "$a" >/tmp/h.ro 2>/tmp/h.re ); echo "ref=$?"; ( ulimit -v 2000000; timeout 30 /output/test11 "$a" >/tmp/h.uo 2>/tmp/h.ue ); echo "rust=$?"; cmp /tmp/h.ro /tmp/h.uo; cmp /tmp/h.re /tmp/h.ue; done   # stdout identical (0B), exit 134 both, stderr differs.  Unconstrained control: ( ulimit -v 90000000; timeout -k 2 20 /workspace/dataset/test11_executable 2147483647 ) -> exit 124, 0B/0B; same for /output/test11 -> exit 124, 0B/0B (both hang, consistent)

SCOPE: CLI/argv fuzzing only. Compared /output/test11 (md5 87824a3787bb3561dc1e19598dd7082a, built 16:24:22 — verified unchanged before and after every sweep) against /workspace/dataset/test11_executable, always on stdout AND stderr AND exit status, using `cmp` on files (never shell string comparison).

IMPORTANT — SOURCES CHANGED MID-SESSION: when I started, /output/test11.rs used `std::env::args()` and /output/cli.rs had no OsString handling. At 16:24 another actor rewrote them to `std::env::args_os()` + `to_string_lossy()` (see the doc comment now at /output/cli.rs:59-66) and rebuilt the binary. I re-ran EVERY sweep from scratch against the post-16:24 binary; all results below are for that binary. I verified with a standalone probe that `std::env::args().nth(1)` on rustc 1.75.0 panics (exit 101) on non-UTF-8 argv, so the pre-16:24 version would have diverged on e.g. argv[1]=$'\\xff7'; the current args_os+lossy version does not.

- /tmp/fuzz/cases.sh + /tmp/fuzz/run.sh — the 41 required argv values as a bash array (so tabs/newlines/trailing spaces survive intact), plus the two extra-arg cases.
- /tmp/fuzz/extra.sh, /tmp/utf8edge.sh, /tmp/long.sh — extended edge cases.
- /tmp/rfuzz.sh + /tmp/gen.c, /tmp/gen2.c — randomized fuzzers (hex-encoded argv so arbitrary bytes round-trip).
- /tmp/atoichk2 (C: prints atoi/strtol/errno) used as an independent oracle for the decoded n of every value.
- /tmp/dump.c to confirm raw bytes actually reach argv.
- /tmp/argc0.c to execve with an empty argv (argc==0).

findings.title: SIGPIPE is ignored by the Rust runtime: early-closed stdout pipe yields exit 0 instead of death by signal 13
findings.location: /output/test11.rs:13 (fn main — no SIGPIPE disposition restored before writing)
findings.detail: The Rust standard library sets SIGPIPE to SIG_IGN during runtime init, and /output/test11.rs never restores SIG_DFL. Every write in the loop is `let _ = write!(...)`, so EPIPE is silently swallowed and the process exits 0. The C++ reference keeps the default SIGPIPE disposition and is killed by signal 13 (shell status 141) on the first write after the reader closes. Observed: `test11_executable 5000 | head -c 10` -> PIPESTATUS[0]=141; `/output/test11 5000 | head -c 10` -> PIPESTATUS[0]=0. The 10 stdout bytes that did get through were byte-identical, and /workspace/difftest.sh redirects stdout to files so it can never surface this, so the impact is confined to exit-status/termination-signal observability rather than stdout content. Fixable with std only (an `extern "C" { fn signal(i32, usize) -> usize; }` declaration plus one call at the top of main); no crate needed. Other write-failure paths were checked and do match: stdout closed (`1>&-`) gives exit 0 / empty stderr on both, and `>/dev/full` gives exit 0 / empty stderr on both, i.e. the Rust does not panic where C++ merely sets badbit.
findings.repro:
/workspace/dataset/test11_executable 5000 | head -c 10 >/dev/null; echo ref=${PIPESTATUS[0]}   # 141
/output/test11 5000 | head -c 10 >/dev/null; echo rust=${PIPESTATUS[0]}   # 0

findings.title: std::env::args() is not used — the code uses args_os() + to_string_lossy (deliberate, and required for correctness)
findings.detail: The review brief asks to verify `std::env::args()` is used; the shipped code calls `std::env::args_os()` and then `arg.to_string_lossy()`. If the requirement is meant literally this is a deviation, but switching to `std::env::args()` would introduce a real divergence: I built a minimal variant in /tmp/argsvar that collects `std::env::args()` and it panics on a non-UTF-8 argv (`thread 'main' panicked at library/std/src/env.rs:807:51: called Result::unwrap() on an Err value: "\xFF7"`, exit 101), whereas the C++ reference happily runs atoi over the raw bytes and exits 0. The lossy conversion is provably behaviour-preserving here because Rust's UTF-8 lossy decoder never consumes an ASCII byte into an invalid subpart, and every byte >= 0x80 (including the U+FFFD replacement's EF BF BD) is neither a C-locale space, a sign, nor a digit, so parsing stops at exactly the same offset. I verified this empirically rather than only by argument: parse_n over all 255 one-byte and all 65025 two-byte argv strings, and 175616 four-byte strings over a byte alphabet chosen to include every isspace char, sign, digits and the full range of UTF-8-invalid lead/continuation bytes (0x7f/0x80/0x9f/0xa0/0xbf/0xc0/0xc3/0xe0/0xef/0xf0/0xf4/0xf5/0xfe/0xff), all identical to glibc atoi. Recommendation: keep args_os; if literal compliance with the wording matters, use `std::os::unix::ffi::OsStrExt::as_bytes()` on the OsStr instead of lossy decoding rather than reverting to args().

bash -c 'exec /tmp/argsvar/demo $'''\xff7'''' ; echo exit=$?   # panics, exit=101
printf '\xff7
\xff
5\xff

\xc35
\xe0\x805
8\xf0\x9f\x92\xa9
' | /workspace/difftest.sh   # checked=9 failures=0 with the shipped args_os version

result.coverage:
Read /workspace/dataset/test11.cpp, /output/cli.rs, /output/test11.rs, /output/gear.rs, /output/earcut/mod.rs, /output/Cargo.toml.

Binary provenance: copied the sources to /tmp/rev, built with `rustc -O test11.rs -o test11_local`; the result is byte-identical to /output/test11 (`cmp` clean), so the shipped binary really is this source.

argc / default: `parse_n` uses `args.nth(1)`, matching `if (argc > 1)`. Verified no-arg (exit 0, 154 bytes, identical to `11`), empty-string argv[1] (== n=0), extra trailing args ignored (`test11 3 extra ignored`), and argc==0 via a C execve helper (/tmp/exec0.c) — both binaries fall back to n=11 and emit identical bytes.

atoi: built a glibc oracle (/tmp/atoi/oracle.c, `atoi` on NUL-separated records) and a harness that calls the real `cli::parse_n` through OsString::from_vec (/tmp/atoi/rust_atoi.rs), then compared: (a) 4249 hand-picked adversarial records (whitespace forms, "  +  5", "--5", "0x10", "5abc", digit runs of length 1..25, plus 4000 random strings over a pool containing \\xff/\\xfe/\\xc3/\\x80/\\t/\\n/\\v/\\f/\\r); (b) exhaustively all 255 one-byte and all 65025 two-byte argv strings; (c) 175616 four-byte strings over a 28-byte alphabet spanning every C isspace char, signs, digits and UTF-8-invalid bytes. All 245145 comparisons identical. Also drove ~450 real invocations of both binaries through /workspace/difftest.sh (seq 1 400, plus the overflow set) — 0 failures. Saturation confirmed end-to-end against the reference by matching `test11_executable <weird-arg>` output against `test11_executable <glibc-atoi-value>` output: 4294967299->3, 8589934595->3, 12345678901->-539222987, 2147483648->-2147483648, 9223372036854775808->-1 (i64-wrap would give 0), 18446744073709551617->-1 (u64-wrap would give 1), -9223372036854775809->0, plus a 100000-digit argument and one with 100000 leading spaces. Reasoned about the one asymmetry in cli.rs (it accumulates positively and negates, so LONG_MIN is reachable only via the saturation branch) and confirmed "-9223372036854775808" still yields 0 like glibc.

Locale: `objdump -T /workspace/dataset/test11_executable` imports strtol and no setlocale, so the process stays in the "C" locale; empirically ran both binaries under LC_ALL/LANG = C, POSIX, C.utf8, en_US.utf8, en_US.iso88591, de_DE.iso88591, fr_FR.iso88591, ru_RU.koi8r, ja_JP.eucjp, tr_TR.iso88599 with argv bytes 0xa0 (NBSP), 0x85 (NEL), 0x1c, 0xff — atoi is 0 in every locale and Rust matches every time. Locale cannot matter here.

Output/IO: `write!(out, "{} ", idx)` over u32 with all errors discarded, explicit flush, no newline. Confirmed no trailing newline by hexdump at n=3, n=11, n=300 and n=100000 (3866640 bytes, ends `... 37855 `). Exit status 0 and empty stderr for n in 0..60 plus 200/1000/5000. Write-failure paths: `1>&-`, `>/dev/full`, and a pty (`script -qec`) all byte- and exit-identical, no panic. Also checked behaviour under `ulimit -v 40000` at n=100000: both exit 0 with identical 3866640-byte stdout. Timing at n=100000: ref 3790 ms vs Rust 4276 ms. The one behavioural gap I found is the SIGPIPE disposition (finding 1). I did not find any input where stdout bytes differ; the only difference C++'s badbit-latching could cause (Rust keeps retrying writes after a failure, C++ stops) needs a write that fails and then later succeeds, which I could not construct and which produces no divergence on /dev/full or a closed fd.
